chapter_title: Functions, Methods, and Basic Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) in C#

screens.title: Functions, Methods, and Basic OOP in C#
screens.subtitle: Encapsulate behavior, pass data, and connect components safely inside Unity scripts

narration.text: In this chapter we'll learn why methods and simple object-oriented patterns matter for game scripting. Methods let you package a single task—like taking damage or calculating distance—into one reusable block, which keeps code tidy and prevents duplication as your project grows. You'll see how to pass parameters and return values so methods become flexible tools, and how method overloading gives you multiple ways to call the same logical action. We'll also introduce core OOP ideas: classes as blueprints, objects as instances, and access modifiers that control what other scripts can use. Practically, you'll apply these ideas in Unity with GetComponent calls and learn to guard against the common NullReferenceException with null checks. Throughout, we focus on concrete examples you can try right away: a PlayerHealth class, a DamageDealer trigger, and splitting a long Update loop into smaller methods. By the end you'll be able to design small, testable components and wire them together cleanly in Unity. Think about one part of your current code that repeats: could a single method replace those repeated lines?

keyIdea.title: Modular, testable game code
keyIdea.text: Use methods and simple OOP to encapsulate behavior, make code reusable, and let components communicate safely with GetComponent and null checks.

Functions, Methods, and Basic OOP in C#

Learn to write small reusable methods, pass parameters, return values, and structure small classes so your Unity scripts are easier to read, reuse, and debug. We'll practice GetComponent and common defensive patterns used in Unity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after completing this chapter

narration.text: By the end of these lessons you'll be able to define and call custom methods in C#, and explain why encapsulation matters. You will practice adding parameters to methods so the same code can operate on different inputs, and returning values when you need computed results. You will also recognize method overloading and when it simplifies APIs for other developers. On the practical side, you'll create a small PlayerHealth class, move health logic into clear methods, and use GetComponent to connect scripts at runtime. These skills let you refactor long Update loops into readable, testable steps and reduce bugs that come from duplicated logic. For each objective we give a quick mnemonic and a micro milestone you can verify in the editor. Keep in mind that understanding methods is not just syntax; it is about designing clearer responsibilities in your code so teammates can work on different systems independently.

screens.title: What is a Method (Function) in C#?
screens.subtitle: Definition, role, and a concrete Unity example

narration.text: A method is a named block of code that performs a specific task and can be invoked from other places in your script. In Unity C#, methods let you isolate repeated behavior—such as applying damage, playing an animation, or calculating a distance—so that the logic lives in one place. Defining a method requires a return type, a name, and an optional parameter list. For example, a TakeDamage method takes an integer amount and adjusts player health; that single method can be called from input handling, collision triggers, or enemy attacks. This encapsulation reduces duplicated lines and makes each part of your code easier to inspect and test. A common misconception is that methods are only for complex logic; in fact, even small repeated statements benefit from being moved into a small method because it documents intent and simplifies debugging. Concrete example: the PlayerCombat. TakeDamage(int damageAmount) method subtracts health, clamps it to zero, and calls Die when health reaches zero. When you call that method from many places, you avoid forgetting the health clamp or the death check. Key takeaway: pick one clear responsibility for each method and keep it short. How might you split a long Update into three focused methods today?

keyIdea.title: Method = single responsibility
keyIdea.text: A method should do one well-defined task so you can reuse and test that behavior consistently across your project.

content.html:
Core Concept

Method definition

A method encapsulates a single task and can accept parameters or return a value. Small methods make code easier to read and maintain.

  • Return type: void or a data type like int/float/Vector3.
  • Parameters: inputs that change behavior without editing the method body.
  • Call sites: methods are invoked where the behavior is needed, reducing duplication.
Key Takeaway

One responsibility per method makes intent clear and prevents duplicated logic across your scripts.

// Example from PlayerCombat
public void TakeDamage(int damageAmount)
{
    playerHealth -= damageAmount;
    if (playerHealth < 0) playerHealth = 0;
    Debug.Log("Player took " + damageAmount + " damage. Current Health: " + playerHealth);

    if (playerHealth == 0)
    {
        Die();
    }
}

private void Die()
{
    Debug.Log("Player has died!");
    gameObject.SetActive(false);
}
Concrete example
Call TakeDamage from an input event, an enemy script, or a trigger to centralize death logic and health clamping.
Common mistake: forgetting to clamp health or to call Die consistently when health reaches zero. Moving that logic into one method prevents the bug.

screens.title: Parameters and Return Values
screens.subtitle: How methods accept inputs and produce outputs for flexible behavior

narration.text: Parameters let a method act on specific data you provide at call time; return values let it compute a result and hand it back. When you design a method, think about the minimal inputs it needs and a clear return type. For example, a CalculateDistance method takes two Vector3 positions and returns a float. That return can be used by other systems to decide whether an enemy is within attack range. A practical pattern is to keep side effects controlled: if a method returns a value, prefer not to also change unrelated global state unless that side effect is the method's explicit purpose. A common misconception is that more parameters always make a method powerful. In fact, too many parameters signal a need to split responsibilities or create a small value object. Concrete example from the chapter: CalculateDistance(Vector3 point1, Vector3 point2) returns Vector3. Distance, which a caller stores in a float then compares against attackRange. Also remember that a method with a non-void return type must return a value on every code path; forgetting this causes a compile error. Try to write methods that return small, predictable types and keep complex mutation in clearly named void methods.

keyIdea.title: Inputs and outputs
keyIdea.text: Design methods with minimal parameters and explicit return values; avoid mixing many side effects with returned results for clearer APIs.

content.html:
Definition

Parameters & return values

Parameters accept data; returns produce computed results. Use them to separate computation from side effects.

public float CalculateDistance(Vector3 point1, Vector3 point2)
{
    return Vector3.Distance(point1, point2);
}

// Usage
float distance = CalculateDistance(transform.position, enemyPosition);
if (distance < attackRange) { Debug.Log("Enemy is within attack range!"); }
Pro tip
Return small types for predictability; use out or tuples sparingly for grouped returns.
Common mistake
Forgetting to return a value on every path causes a compile error for non-void methods.
Example scenario

Use CalculateDistance in enemy AI to decide when to switch from wandering to attacking. Keep the distance check separate from the attack method.

Key Takeaway

Separate calculation (returns) from actions (void methods) to keep code predictable and testable.

screens.title: Method Overloading
screens.subtitle: Offer multiple signatures for the same action

narration.text: Method overloading means defining multiple methods that share a name but differ in their parameter lists. This gives a single logical action several convenient ways to be called. For example, an Attack method can be overloaded: a parameterless Attack performs a default strike, Attack(float damageMultiplier) applies a scaled value, and Attack(GameObject target) applies logic to a specific enemy. Overloading improves A P I ergonomics: teammates can call the form that best matches their context without writing adapter code. But misuse is possible. If your overloaded methods do very different things, you lose clarity and make maintenance harder. A good rule is to overload only when each variant performs a related operation with similar semantics. Concrete example from PlayerCombat: having three Attack signatures helps the animator or AI invoke attacks without constructing complex argument sets. A misconception is to overload by changing only the return type; C# does not allow that. When in doubt, prefer descriptive method names rather than excessive overloads. Method Overloading means use overloading to provide natural calling options for the same logical action, but avoid making variants that diverge in meaning.. In practical terms, offer multiple signatures for the same action. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Overload with purpose
keyIdea.text: Use overloading to provide natural calling options for the same logical action, but avoid making variants that diverge in meaning.

content.html:
Comparison

Overloaded vs separate names

Overload when variants are semantically the same. If behavior differs substantially, pick a new method name.

// Overloaded examples
public void Attack()
{
    Debug.Log("Player performs a basic attack!");
}

public void Attack(float damageMultiplier)
{
    Debug.Log("Player performs a boosted attack with multiplier: " + damageMultiplier);
}

public void Attack(GameObject target)
{
    Debug.Log("Player attacks " + target.name + "!");
}
When to prefer overloads
  • Variants share the same intent and side effects.
  • Variants differ only by optional extra data or specificity.
  • Avoid overloads that change outcome semantics drastically.
Pitfall
Attempting to overload only by return type is not allowed in C#; signatures must differ in parameter lists.

screens.title: Classes and Objects: Blueprints and Instances
screens.subtitle: How a script becomes a component instance in Unity

narration.text: A class is a blueprint that defines data and behavior for a type of object. In Unity, a C# script that inherits from MonoBehaviour becomes a class that can be attached to a GameObject. When you attach the script, Unity creates an instance of that class for the specific GameObject, and that instance holds its own field values like playerHealth or attackRange. This distinction is important: changing a field on one instance does not change it on another instance unless you explicitly share a static value. A common misconception is to treat a class as a single global object; instead, think in terms of many small instances cooperating. For example, multiple enemies can have their own PlayerCombat components with separate health values and behaviors even though they share the same class definition. Understanding instances helps you reason about state, lifetime, and when to cache references versus when to query a component each time. Consider whether a value belongs to the class blueprint or to each instance when designing your component APIs. Classes and Objects: Blueprints and Instances means classes describe capability; each gameobject with the script is a distinct instance with its own state.. In practical terms, how a script becomes a component instance in unity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Blueprint vs instance
keyIdea.text: Classes describe capability; each GameObject with the script is a distinct instance with its own state.

content.html:
Definition

Class vs Object

A class is a template; an object is a concrete instance created when the script is attached to a GameObject.

  • Class defines fields and methods.
  • Each instance has its own field values and lifecycle.
  • Use static only when a value should be shared across all instances.
Example: PlayerCombat class
Attach PlayerCombat to multiple GameObjects and each will maintain separate playerHealth values and behavior.
Key Takeaway

Design whether state is per instance or shared. Use instances to keep per-GameObject behavior isolated and predictable.

screens.title: Access Modifiers: public, private, protected, internal
screens.subtitle: Control visibility and protect internal logic

narration.text: Access modifiers determine who can see and use members of a class. The most common modifiers in Unity scripting are public and private. Public members are accessible from other classes and show up in the Inspector, which is useful for designer-tweakable values and inter-component communication. Private members are only accessible within the class; use them to hide internal state and prevent accidental modification. Protected allows derived classes to access a member while keeping it hidden from others; internal limits access to the same assembly. A frequent beginner mistake is making many fields public to access them from other scripts; this exposes implementation details and makes future refactoring risky. Instead, prefer public properties or methods that encapsulate access when necessary. For example, keep playerHealth private and provide a public method or property to apply damage or read current health. This protects invariants like clamping health between zero and maxHealth. Access Modifiers: public, private, protected, internal means expose only what other systems need. use private for internal state and public methods or properties for controlled interaction.. In practical terms, control visibility and protect internal logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Encapsulation with modifiers
keyIdea.text: Expose only what other systems need. Use private for internal state and public methods or properties for controlled interaction.

content.html:
Core Concept

Access modifiers

Control who can read or change your fields and methods. Encapsulation reduces bugs and future refactor pain.

  • public: visible everywhere, appears in Inspector.
  • private: visible only inside the class.
  • protected/internal: for inheritance or same-assembly access.
Practical pattern

Keep data private. Offer public methods like TakeDamage or Heal to mutate state while preserving invariants like clamping.

Pro tip
Expose only what designers or other systems need. Use [SerializeField] on private fields if you want editor visibility without public access.

screens.title: GetComponent<T>() Pattern and Null Checking
screens.subtitle: Find and use components safely at runtime

narration.text: GetComponent is the standard way to find another component on the same GameObject. In Awake or Start you typically cache a reference by calling GetComponent and storing the result in a field; this is efficient and reduces repeated lookups. However, GetComponent can return null if the component is not present, leading to a NullReferenceException when you try to use it. The safe pattern is: get the component, check for null, and log an error or disable dependent features if it's missing. For example, in Awake assign playerRigidbody = GetComponent (); then if playerRigidbody is null, log an error so you know the object is misconfigured. A common alternative is FindObjectOfType, which searches the whole scene; it is convenient but slower and often unnecessary when the component lives on the same GameObject. Concrete example: a DamageDealer uses GetComponent () on the colliding object and only calls TakeDamage if the returned reference is not null. This simple defense prevents common runtime crashes and makes debugging clearer. GetComponent<T>() Pattern and Null Checking means cache components with getcomponent in awake/start and always check for null to avoid nullreferenceexception at runtime.. In practical terms, find and use components safely at runtime. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Safe component references
keyIdea.text: Cache components with GetComponent in Awake/Start and always check for null to avoid NullReferenceException at runtime.

content.html:
Pattern

GetComponent & null checks

Cache components early and guard usage with a null check to keep your game from crashing at runtime.

void Awake()
{
    playerRigidbody = GetComponent();
    if (playerRigidbody == null)
    {
        Debug.LogError("Rigidbody component not found on this GameObject!");
    }
}

void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
{
    PlayerHealth ph = other.GetComponent();
    if (ph != null) ph.TakeDamage(damageAmount);
}
Example: DamageDealer

When a collider enters the damage zone, attempt to get PlayerHealth. If null, do nothing. If present, call TakeDamage so only valid players are affected.

Common mistake
Skipping null checks leads to NullReferenceException and often a confusing crash in the console. Add early checks and helpful error logs.

screens.title: Refactoring Update() into Smaller Methods
screens.subtitle: Organize input, movement, and state changes into focused methods

narration.text: Long Update methods become difficult to read and maintain. Refactoring means splitting Update into smaller, clearly named methods such as HandleInput, ApplyDamage, and UpdateAnimations. Each method has a focused responsibility and can be tested independently. Start by identifying repeated or logically distinct sections in Update, then extract them. For example, move input processing into HandleInput, health logic into ApplyDamage or TakeDamage, and physics interactions into FixedUpdate or a separate PhysicsUpdate method. A useful pattern is to make the extracted methods public or private based on whether other classes need to call them. Another misconception is thinking refactoring changes behavior; when done carefully you only move code, keeping behavior identical while improving readability. Concrete example: take a block that checks for key presses and calls TakeDamage and move it into a HandleDebugInput method. After extraction, Update becomes a clear sequence of steps, which is especially helpful when you come back days later or when other developers read your code. Refactoring Update() into Smaller Methods means break complex update logic into small methods to make flow explicit and reduce duplication, helping debugging and collaboration.. In practical terms, organize input, movement, and state changes into focused methods. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor for clarity
keyIdea.text: Break complex Update logic into small methods to make flow explicit and reduce duplication, helping debugging and collaboration.

content.html:
Process

Refactor Update()

  1. 1. Identify logical blocks inside Update (input, movement, health).
  2. 2. Extract each block into a named method like HandleInput().
  3. 3. Move physics to FixedUpdate if appropriate and test behavior.
Concrete example
Before: a single Update handling input, damage keys, and animation. After: Update calls HandleInput(), UpdateMovement(), and SyncAnimation(). Each method is short and self-documenting.
Key Takeaway

Small methods reveal intent and make it safe to change behavior without introducing regressions.

screens.title: PlayerHealth and DamageDealer Walkthrough
screens.subtitle: Implementing interactions with methods and GetComponent

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks through creating a PlayerHealth component and a DamageDealer trigger that interacts with it. PlayerHealth stores currentHealth and maxHealth and exposes TakeDamage and Heal methods. TakeDamage subtracts the amount, clamps the value to zero, and calls a private Die method when health reaches zero. DamageDealer is attached to a trigger collider and in OnTriggerEnter it attempts to get the PlayerHealth component from the colliding GameObject. If PlayerHealth is present, DamageDealer calls TakeDamage with a specified damageAmount. This pattern shows the full loop: encapsulate health rules in one class, and let other objects interact via a clear method. When implementing, remember to add a Rigidbody (isKinematic) and a trigger collider to the DamageZone so OnTriggerEnter fires. Test by moving the player into the zone and watching the Debug. Log messages. A common mistake is using new PlayerHealth() instead of GetComponent, which creates an unattached instance and won't affect the in-scene GameObject. Use GetComponent and null checks for safety. PlayerHealth and DamageDealer Walkthrough means encapsulate health changes in playerhealth and let damagedealer call its methods via getcomponent with a null check to ensure safe runtime behavior.. In practical terms, implementing interactions with methods and getcomponent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Activity: component interaction
keyIdea.text: Encapsulate health changes in PlayerHealth and let DamageDealer call its methods via GetComponent with a null check to ensure safe runtime behavior.

content.html:
Activity

Implement PlayerHealth & DamageDealer

public class PlayerHealth : MonoBehaviour
{
    public int currentHealth = 100;
    public int maxHealth = 100;

    public void TakeDamage(int amount)
    {
        currentHealth -= amount;
        if (currentHealth < 0) currentHealth = 0;
        Debug.Log("Player took " + amount + " damage. Current Health: " + currentHealth);
        if (currentHealth == 0) Die();
    }

    private void Die() { Debug.Log("Player has been defeated!"); gameObject.SetActive(false); }
}

public class DamageDealer : MonoBehaviour
{
    public int damageAmount = 25;
    void OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)
    {
        PlayerHealth playerHealth = other.GetComponent();
        if (playerHealth != null) playerHealth.TakeDamage(damageAmount);
    }
}
Testing checklist
  • Add PlayerHealth to a player GameObject.
  • Create DamageZone with BoxCollider (Is Trigger) and Rigidbody (Is Kinematic).
  • Attach DamageDealer and set damageAmount, then run and observe Debug.Log messages.
Common mistake
Do not use new PlayerHealth(); it creates an unattached instance instead of the component on the GameObject.

screens.title: GetComponent vs FindObjectOfType vs new
screens.subtitle: When to use each approach for getting references

narration.text: There are three common ways beginners try to access components: GetComponent on the same GameObject, FindObjectOfType that searches the scene, and creating a new instance with new. GetComponent is the most direct and efficient when the component lives on the same GameObject. Cache it in Awake or Start for repeated use. FindObjectOfType can be convenient for singletons or manager objects, but it scans the scene and can be slow or ambiguous if multiple matches exist. Using new for MonoBehaviour-derived scripts does not create a component attached to a GameObject and will not run with Unity's lifecycle methods; it simply constructs a plain C# object and is almost always wrong for MonoBehaviours. A common misconception is that new attaches a script to the scene—this is false. Use AddComponent to create a component on a GameObject at runtime if you need to dynamically add behavior. For most inter-component calls inside the same GameObject, GetComponent plus null checking is the right choice. GetComponent vs FindObjectOfType vs new means prefer getcomponent for same-object references, use findobjectoftype sparingly, and never use new for monobehaviours; use addcomponent when you need a runtime-attached component.. In practical terms, when to use each approach for getting references. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Choose reference patterns
keyIdea.text: Prefer GetComponent for same-object references, use FindObjectOfType sparingly, and never use new for MonoBehaviours; use AddComponent when you need a runtime-attached component.

content.html:
Comparison

GetComponent vs alternatives

GetComponent
Efficient for same GameObject; cache in Awake/Start and null-check.
FindObjectOfType
Searches scene; use sparingly for singletons or editors, not for high-frequency lookup.
new vs AddComponent
new does not create an attached component. Use AddComponent<T> to attach a component at runtime.
Practical advice
  • Cache GetComponent results when you need them repeatedly.
  • Avoid FindObjectOfType in performance-sensitive code.
  • Use AddComponent when you intentionally need a runtime-attached component.
Key Takeaway

Pick the right reference strategy: efficiency and correctness matter more than convenience when wiring components.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Defensive Patterns
screens.subtitle: Null checks, missing returns, and improper access

narration.text: Some mistakes recur when learning methods and OOP in Unity. First, forgetting to return a value from a non-void method causes a compile error. Second, trying to access private members from another class causes a visibility error at compile time; use public methods or properties for controlled access. Third, assuming GetComponent always returns a valid reference leads to NullReferenceException at runtime. The defensive patterns are simple: always return a value from non-void methods on every code path; respect access modifiers and expose behavior via methods instead of changing fields directly; and null-check GetComponent results and log helpful errors if a required component is missing. Another helpful habit is to centralize object pooling, damage calculation, or health clamping so behavior is not accidentally duplicated across scripts. Concrete example: if TakeDamage should never reduce health below zero, put that clamp in TakeDamage and never perform manual subtraction in other scripts. These small habits prevent bugs and make it easier for teammates to reason about your code. Common Mistakes and Defensive Patterns means adopt simple checks and encapsulation: return values, respect access modifiers, and always null-check component references to avoid runtime errors.. In practical terms, null checks, missing returns, and improper access. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Defensive coding
keyIdea.text: Adopt simple checks and encapsulation: return values, respect access modifiers, and always null-check component references to avoid runtime errors.

content.html:
Pitfalls

Common mistakes to avoid

  • Missing return in non-void methods — compile-time error.
  • Accessing private members externally — respect encapsulation.
  • Using new for MonoBehaviours — does not attach the component to the scene.
  • Not null-checking GetComponent results — runtime NullReferenceException.
Defensive checklist
Return on every path for non-void methods, use public methods to mutate private state, cache required components and verify they exist with helpful logs.
Key Takeaway

Small defensive habits prevent confusing errors and make your Unity projects more robust and maintainable.

narration.text: Let's summarize the most important ideas you should carry forward. First, a Method or Function packages a single, reusable task; prefer short methods with one responsibility. Second, DRY stands for Don't Repeat Yourself: centralize repeated logic into methods so fixes happen once. Third, Parameters are inputs and Return Values are outputs; design methods so they accept minimal input and return explicit results. These concepts guide how you split logic, how you refactor Update loops, and how other developers will read your code. As you practice, test each method in isolation and prefer clear names that describe intent. Carry these habits into your Unity projects and you'll reduce bugs and speed up collaboration. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Short methods, DRY design, and clear parameter/return contracts form the basis of maintainable game code.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Key Concepts

narration.text: Finish with practical patterns you will use repeatedly: use GetComponent and cache references in Awake or Start, always null-check component results, and avoid new for MonoBehaviours. Prefer AddComponent when you need to create a runtime-attached component. Respect access modifiers: make fields private and expose behavior through public methods so you keep internal invariants intact. Finally, practice refactoring: move repeated code into methods and split long Update methods into focused steps. These habits make your Unity projects robust, easier to debug, and faster to extend. As a reflection, ask yourself: which repeated behavior in your current project should become a method today? Key Concepts — Part 2 means cache and null-check component references, avoid incorrect instantiation, and use access control to protect internal logic.. In practical terms, practical unity patterns and defensive habits. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 1.4 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts

GetComponent
Retrieve components on a GameObject; always check for null.
Access modifiers
Use private to hide internals and public methods to expose behavior safely.
Refactor Update()
Split responsibilities into named methods to improve readability and testability.
Final Takeaway

Adopt small, testable methods, use clear visibility rules, and wire components safely. These patterns will save time and reduce bugs as your game grows.

ai_generation_note:
Create a 15-minute live coding video. Start by refactoring a single, long `Update()` method into several smaller, focused methods (e.g., `HandleInput()`, `ApplyDamage()`). Demonstrate how to define methods with parameters and return types, showing how to pass values and use returned results. Introduce method overloading with a practical example like `Heal(int amount)` and `Heal(int amount, bool overHealAllowed)`. Explain OOP concepts by showing how `PlayerHealth` is a class and an instance on a GameObject is an object. Then, implement the `GetComponent<T>()` pattern by having a `DamageDealer` script find and call `TakeDamage()` on a `PlayerHealth` script on a colliding GameObject. Emphasize the importance of null checks after `GetComponent()`. Use a split-screen view with the code editor and Unity Editor (showing GameObject components and console output). Include a reflection prompt for learners to consider how they could further modularize their `PlayerManager` script.
